paragraphs: This paper asks how smoothly a model can fit noisy training examples exactly. Smoothness is measured through a Lipschitz constant: larger values permit greater changes in predictions between nearby inputs. Earlier understanding relied on a particular distributional property called isoperimetry. The authors instead study arbitrary data distributions supported on a bounded space.

For a neural network with p parameters fitting n examples, they prove a Lipschitz lower bound of order square root of n/p. This establishes a constraint on how smooth an interpolating network can be and validates a prior conjecture for two-layer networks with polynomial weights. Increasing parameter count can relax this particular constraint.

They also establish a lower bound of order n raised to 1/d for arbitrary interpolating approximators in dimension d. Together, the results identify two regimes: overparameterization may help smooth interpolation when sample size is polynomial in dimension, while a constant Lipschitz bound becomes impossible when sample size grows as exp(ω(d)). The benefit of extra parameters therefore coexists with a broader distribution-independent obstruction.
icml-2023-a-law-of-robustness-beyond-iso.tldr: Two lower bounds reveal when extra parameters may help smooth interpolation and when sample growth rules out constant-Lipschitz interpolation.

paragraphs: Continual meta-learning involves learning from a sequence of tasks, each with few examples, while developing knowledge useful for later tasks. When tasks differ substantially, mixture models can maintain different components of this shared knowledge. The paper identifies two sources of parameter inefficiency: treating components as mutually exclusive and allowing the collection to grow without removing redundancy.

Adaptive Compositional Continual Meta-Learning, or ACML, associates each task with a subset of components. This lets different tasks reuse overlapping combinations of knowledge. The compositional premise matters because heterogeneous tasks can still share useful elements, even when assigning them to a single exclusive component would obscure that overlap.

ACML also uses component sparsification based on evidential theory to filter out redundant components and adapt the number retained. Experiments show improvements over strong baselines and support the effectiveness of compositional meta-knowledge. The stated contribution combines two forms of adaptation: changing how tasks share existing knowledge and adjusting which components remain useful as tasks arrive.
icml-2023-adaptive-compositional-continu.tldr: ACML shares combinations of meta-knowledge across sequential few-shot tasks and removes redundant components to adapt its capacity.

paragraphs: Federated learning often proceeds with only some clients participating in each round. When clients have different data, missing updates can make the combined model update diverge from what full participation would produce. Large local batches have been proposed to address heterogeneity, but their usefulness under partial participation is less clear.

FedAMD divides participating clients into anchor and miner groups. Anchor clients compute large-batch gradients to establish local reference directions, described as bullseyes. Miner clients use those references to guide multiple small-batch local updates and contribute to the global model. The design gives large and small batches complementary roles within the same training framework.

For non-convex objectives, the authors report convergence with up to an O(1/ε) reduction in communication rounds relative to state-of-the-art methods, measured by ε-approximation. Experiments on real-world datasets also report lower computation and communication costs alongside improved test accuracy. These findings support anchor sampling as a way to make partial participation more effective while reducing the resources needed for training.
icml-2023-anchor-sampling-for-federated-.tldr: FedAMD combines large-batch anchor gradients with guided small-batch updates to improve federated learning under partial client participation.

paragraphs: Truncated density estimation concerns probability models restricted to a particular region. Fitting these models is difficult because their normalizing constants can be intractable and their boundaries impose demanding conditions. Adapted score-matching methods require a weighting function that vanishes at the boundary while remaining positive inside, making the boundary itself a practical obstacle.

The authors introduce approximate Stein classes, which produce a relaxed version of a Stein identity. They use this construction to define truncated kernelised Stein discrepancy, or TKSD. Its key practical feature is that it can be evaluated using boundary samples without choosing a weighting function in advance or requiring an explicit formula for the boundary.

The density model is fitted by minimizing TKSD's Lagrangian dual. This changes how boundary information enters estimation: sampled boundary locations can replace the explicit boundary description needed by the earlier weighting-function approach. Experiments report better estimation accuracy than previous work even without the boundary's functional form, supporting the usefulness of the relaxed construction in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-approximate-stein-classes-for-.tldr: TKSD estimates truncated densities using boundary samples, avoiding a predefined weighting function and an explicit boundary formula.

paragraphs: Explaining a language model causally requires asking how its output would change under an appropriate counterfactual input. For an observed text, the exact counterfactual texts needed to isolate representation effects are unavailable. The paper investigates whether approximate counterfactuals can still support robust causal explanations, instead of abandoning counterfactual information altogether.

Its central proposal is the Causal Proxy Model, or CPM. A CPM learns to reproduce a black-box model's ordinary input-output behavior while developing internal representations that can be intervened on. Those interventions are trained to simulate the black box's counterfactual behavior. Approximate counterfactual texts can come from human-written edits or sampling heuristics guided by metadata.

This gives the proxy two connected responsibilities: matching factual predictions and supporting meaningful interventions for explanation. The authors also find that their best CPM makes factual predictions comparably to the original model. That result supports the possibility of deploying the proxy itself, making the model used for prediction more explainable while retaining comparable factual performance in the reported comparison.
icml-2023-causal-proxy-models-for-concep.tldr: Causal Proxy Models use approximate counterfactual texts to imitate black-box predictions and support interventions for causal explanation.

paragraphs: Asynchronous coordinate updates allow different parts of a computation to advance without all updates occurring together. Delays are therefore part of the problem the algorithm must handle. This paper introduces DEGAS, a delay-agnostic method for computing operator fixed points: solutions that remain unchanged when the relevant operator is applied.

The fixed-point formulation provides a common framework for asynchronous optimization. In particular, the proposed method includes new asynchronous versions of ADMM and block-coordinate descent as special cases. This matters because the contribution extends beyond a single optimization procedure, connecting several update schemes through the same algorithmic construction.

The authors prove convergence for both bounded and unbounded delays under delay-free parameter conditions. They also provide theoretical and experimental evidence that DEGAS adapts to the delays actually encountered. Numerical classification experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. The central result is therefore a combination of convergence guarantees that do not require delay-dependent parameter conditions and evidence that the algorithm responds well to actual asynchronous execution.
icml-2023-delay-agnostic-asynchronous-co.tldr: DEGAS provides asynchronous fixed-point updates with convergence guarantees for bounded and unbounded delays under delay-free parameter conditions.

paragraphs: Scientific simulations often offer several fidelity levels, trading computational cost against output quality. Multi-fidelity active learning seeks to predict the highest-fidelity outputs while choosing useful data from multiple levels. The challenge is to benefit from cheaper simulations without allowing their inaccuracies to dominate the more accurate prediction task.

The paper identifies two obstacles in existing approaches. Gaussian-process methods struggle to scale to high-dimensional data, while some deep methods organize hidden representations into a hierarchy that passes information only from lower to higher fidelity. That one-way structure can propagate errors from lower-fidelity representations into higher-fidelity ones.

Disentangled Multi-fidelity Deep Bayesian Active Learning, or D-MFDAL, instead learns surrogate models conditioned on distributions of functions at multiple fidelities. The proposal targets the restrictive information structure of earlier deep approaches while retaining the goal of selective data acquisition. On surrogate-learning benchmarks involving heat equations, Poisson's equation, and fluid simulations, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both prediction accuracy and sample efficiency.
icml-2023-disentangled-multi-fidelity-de.tldr: D-MFDAL learns from multiple simulation fidelities and reports improved prediction accuracy and sample efficiency on PDE surrogate benchmarks.

paragraphs: Topic models aim to discover meaningful themes and describe how documents relate to them. A recurring failure is topic collapse: several learned topics become semantically similar, producing repetitive themes and leaving other content insufficiently represented. This damages interpretability because an apparently varied collection of topics may contain little actual semantic diversity.

The proposed Embedding Clustering Regularization Topic Model, or ECRTM, adds a clustering regularizer to the existing reconstruction objective. It makes each topic embedding the center of a separately aggregated cluster of word embeddings. Organizing topics around separate word clusters encourages each topic to capture distinct meanings while keeping its words semantically related.

The intended result is both diversity across topics and coherence within each topic, together with useful document-level topic distributions. Benchmark experiments report that ECRTM alleviates topic collapse and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on topic quality, document topic distributions, and downstream classification. These findings connect the embedding-space organization to improvements in both interpretable topic discovery and the usefulness of the resulting document representations.
icml-2023-effective-neural-topic-modelin.tldr: ECRTM organizes word embeddings into separate topic-centered clusters to reduce repetitive topics and improve topic quality.

paragraphs: Most deep forecasting approaches described in this paper belong to the historical-value family, using past observations to predict future values. Time-index models offer another formulation, representing a series through its time coordinate. This has the attractive property of accommodating the continuous nature of the underlying dynamics, but has received comparatively little attention.

Simply replacing a classical, manually specified time function with a more expressive deep network does not solve forecasting. The authors identify a lack of inductive bias as the obstacle: a flexible time-index model can fail to generalize to time steps it has never seen. Expressiveness alone therefore does not supply the structure needed for extrapolation.

DeepTime addresses this issue through a meta-optimization framework for learning deep time-index models. The framework is presented as yielding an efficient and accurate forecaster that overcomes the shortcomings of naive versions. Extensive real-world experiments on long-sequence forecasting report results competitive with state-of-the-art methods and high efficiency, supporting time-index modeling as a practical alternative within the evaluated forecasting setting.
icml-2023-learning-deep-time-index-model.tldr: DeepTime uses meta-optimization to make deep time-index models generalize to unseen time steps for efficient forecasting.

paragraphs: This paper studies why a variational autoencoder's optimization landscape can favor sparse representations. Much earlier theory used an affine decoder, reducing the model to probabilistic PCA. The authors instead analyze a more expressive single-layer decoder for continuous data from multiple-response regression models, placing the analysis in the setting of difficult, NP-hard inverse problems.

They prove conditions under which every minimum of the VAE objective, whether local or global, produces an optimally sparse latent representation. Here, optimal sparsity means reconstructing the data with zero error while using the smallest possible number of active latent dimensions. The guarantee is conditional on the analyzed setting and the established conditions.

The explanation centers on marginalization over the latent posterior, which selectively smooths away bad local minima. The authors contrast this behavior with deterministic autoencoders of equivalent capacity: even with sparsity-promoting regularization, those models retain bad local minima. The result gives a concrete theoretical account of how the VAE objective can support recovery of compact structure beyond the simplified probabilistic-PCA regime.
icml-2023-marginalization-is-not-margina.tldr: Under proved conditions, a studied VAE has only minima that recover optimally sparse representations because marginalization removes bad minima.

paragraphs: Masked Trajectory Models learn by reconstructing a trajectory from randomly selected visible parts of that same trajectory. A trajectory can contain states and actions, so the missing information can correspond to different sequential decision-making questions. Highly varied masking during training encourages one network to handle multiple kinds of reconstruction.

At inference time, choosing a mask determines the network's role. The same learned weights can serve as a forward dynamics model, an inverse dynamics model, or an offline reinforcement-learning agent. The approach makes these capabilities different uses of a shared model rather than requiring a separately trained network for each function.

Experiments on several continuous-control tasks show that the same MTM network can match or outperform specialized networks for these roles. Its learned state representations also significantly accelerate traditional reinforcement-learning algorithms in the reported experiments. On offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks, MTM is competitive with specialized algorithms despite using a generic self-supervised objective without explicit reinforcement-learning components. The findings support masked reconstruction as a versatile source of decision-making capabilities.
icml-2023-masked-trajectory-models-for-p.tldr: MTM learns multiple prediction and control capabilities through masked trajectory reconstruction, selecting each role with an inference-time mask.

paragraphs: Distilling a graph neural network into a multilayer perceptron aims to combine a teacher's topology-aware knowledge with a student's efficient inference. This paper asks whether every node provides equally reliable supervision. It focuses on the quality of individual knowledge points, an aspect that can be obscured when teacher outputs are treated uniformly.

The authors measure reliability through how invariant a node's information entropy remains under noise perturbations. They observe that knowledge points differ both in how quickly they are distilled and in where they occur within the graph. Knowledge-inspired Reliable Distillation, or KRD, uses these observations to model each node's probability of being informative and reliable.

KRD samples additional reliable knowledge points as supervision for student MLPs. Averaged over seven datasets and three GNN architectures, the authors report a 12.62% improvement over vanilla MLPs and a 2.16% improvement over the corresponding teacher GNNs. These results support selecting supervision according to reliability and show that the reported students can exceed their teachers on average in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-quantifying-the-knowledge-in-g.tldr: KRD selects reliable node-level knowledge for distillation, improving student MLP performance beyond the corresponding teachers on average in its experiments.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network often means identifying which part of an input graph most strongly determines its prediction. This paper builds on the observation that graphs commonly share recurring motifs. It proposes using those shared structures to find explanatory subgraphs through non-parametric matching, offering an alternative to prevailing parametric explainers.

MatchExplainer pairs a target graph with counterpart instances and searches for a crucial shared substructure. It does so by minimizing a distance based on node correspondences. The comparison between instances is central: recurring structure provides the basis for identifying the graph portion that serves as the explanation.

The authors also introduce MatchDrop to address false positive sampling in graph sampling or node-dropping approaches. MatchDrop preserves the portion identified as most informative and applies augmentation to the less informative remainder. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report substantial improvements over the compared state-of-the-art parametric explainers. They also show that MatchDrop can enhance GNN performance, connecting explanation-derived structure to a practical graph augmentation strategy.
icml-2023-rethinking-explaining-graph-ne.tldr: MatchExplainer finds explanatory graph structures by matching instances, and MatchDrop preserves those structures during augmentation.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning depends on the views of a graph presented during training. Those views influence which information the resulting representation retains. The paper argues that random corruption or learned view generation can discard essential information or change semantics, motivating an anchor view intended to preserve the graph's essential content.

The authors derive a definition of this anchor view using graph information bottleneck theory. In their formulation, a view that retains essential information should have minimal structural uncertainty. They then use structural entropy to guide its implementation, producing the SEGA anchor view for graph contrastive learning.

The importance of this construction is that view selection becomes tied to an explicit account of structural information. The anchor is intended to provide a meaningful reference for learning representations. Evaluations cover graph classification in unsupervised, semi-supervised, and transfer-learning settings, with significant gains reported over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support the practical value of the proposed anchor across the tested learning arrangements.
icml-2023-sega-structural-entropy-guided.tldr: SEGA uses structural entropy to construct an anchor graph view intended to preserve essential information for contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Sensitivity sampling selects a small representative subset while providing guarantees about approximation quality. A broad existing bound requires a sample count proportional to total sensitivity S times VC dimension d. This paper obtains sharper guarantees for ℓp subspace embeddings beyond the previously understood special case p = 2.

For 1 ≤ p < 2, the authors establish a bound of roughly S^(2/p). For 2 < p < ∞, they obtain roughly S^(2−2/p). They also show tightness of the first bound: some matrices require S^(2/p) samples. That lower bound identifies a genuine obstacle for the sampling method in this range, alongside the improved upper guarantee.

The analysis yields additional bounds for related sampling schemes. Root leverage score sampling needs roughly d samples when 1 ≤ p < 2, while combining leverage score and sensitivity sampling gives roughly d^(2/p)S^(2−4/p) when p > 2. The sensitivity results provide the best known sample complexity for a broad class of structured matrices with small ℓp sensitivity.
icml-2023-sharper-bounds-for-ell-p-sensi.tldr: Sharper sensitivity-sampling bounds reduce sample requirements for ℓp subspace embeddings, with a matching lower bound for 1 ≤ p < 2.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between the inputs and outputs of partial differential equations. The paper argues that learning a complex mapping as a whole in a high-dimensional coordinate space creates difficulties for both accuracy and efficiency. Coupled physical equations make this especially challenging when numerical discretization produces very large representations.

Latent Spectral Models first use an attention-based hierarchical projection network to compress high-dimensional data into a compact latent space in linear time. A neural spectral block then learns multiple basis operators in that space. Inspired by classical spectral methods, the design represents the complex mapping through several learned operator components.

The authors provide theoretical convergence and approximation guarantees for their construction. Across seven benchmarks covering solid and fluid physics, LSM achieves consistent state-of-the-art results and an average relative gain of 11.5%. The contribution connects compact representation learning with a spectral operator design, with the reported experiments supporting this combination as an efficient and accurate approach to the evaluated high-dimensional PDE problems.
icml-2023-solving-high-dimensional-pdes-.tldr: LSM compresses PDE data into a latent space and learns multiple spectral basis operators, reporting gains across seven physics benchmarks.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous treatment-effect estimation asks how a treatment's effect varies across people or groups. Existing approaches often focus on removing confounding caused by imbalanced treatment assignment. The paper highlights another concern: underrepresented populations can still receive unreliable effect estimates, potentially leading to suboptimal treatment choices even when confounding is addressed.

Stable CounterFactual Regression, or StableCFR, combines population rebalancing with confounder balancing. It smooths the population distribution and upsamples underrepresented subpopulations using uniform sampling. Each disjoint subpopulation receives a weight proportional to the Lebesgue measure of its support, tying the weighting to the size of the region it occupies.

StableCFR also uses epsilon-greedy matching to balance covariates between treatment and control groups. These mechanisms address representation within the population and comparability across treatment assignments together. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior treatment-effect estimation for underrepresented populations. The findings support treating insufficient population representation as an explicit part of the estimation problem alongside the usual concern about confounding.
icml-2023-stable-estimation-of-heterogen.tldr: StableCFR combines upsampling of underrepresented populations with covariate matching to improve heterogeneous treatment-effect estimates.

paragraphs: Federated Q-learning combines value estimates learned independently by multiple agents through periodic aggregation. This paper studies infinite-horizon tabular Markov decision processes and provides sample-complexity guarantees for synchronous and asynchronous variants. In both settings, its bounds show a linear speedup with the number of agents and sharper dependence on other problem parameters.

The asynchronous case raises a particular issue: different behavior policies can lead agents to visit very different state-action pairs. Equally averaging their estimates can then be highly suboptimal. Earlier complexity guarantees depend on the least-visited pair across all agents, requiring every individual agent to cover the entire state-action space.

The proposed importance averaging gives greater weight to estimates for more frequently visited state-action pairs. Its improved bound depends instead on the minimum entry of the agents' average occupancy distribution. This changes the coverage requirement to collective coverage: agents may explore different parts of the space, provided their combined experience covers it. Heterogeneity can consequently become useful through complementary exploration.
icml-2023-the-blessing-of-heterogeneity-.tldr: Importance-weighted aggregation lets federated Q-learning benefit from collective state-action coverage while retaining linear speedup guarantees.

paragraphs: An explanation method can assign importance to a feature without establishing that the feature has a statistical relationship with the prediction target. This paper examines that problem through suppressor variables. Such variables can receive substantial importance in explanations despite lacking a target relationship, making the interpretation of an importance score consequential.

The authors move beyond earlier illustrative and empirical observations by deriving analytical expressions for several popular explanation methods. Their setting is a two-dimensional binary classification problem with Gaussian class-conditional distributions. This deliberately simple setup allows the behavior of the methods to be characterized mathematically rather than inferred only from experimental outputs.

For most of the studied approaches, correlated noise leads to nonzero importance for a suppressor feature that is unrelated to the class. The finding places a concrete limit on what these explanations establish: a highlighted feature cannot automatically be interpreted as statistically associated with the target. The demonstrated issue arises within the analyzed setting and concerns the meaning of explanation outputs used for transparency and quality control.
icml-2023-theoretical-behavior-of-xai-me.tldr: In an analyzed Gaussian classification problem, most studied XAI methods assign importance to a class-unrelated suppressor feature under correlated noise.

paragraphs: This paper studies selecting the top k items from m candidates rated by client votes while satisfying differential privacy. Its main resource of interest is data access: how much information an algorithm must retrieve to perform selection. The access model permits both random accesses and accesses through sorted data.

The authors develop an algorithm requiring O(√(mk)) expected accesses, which they identify as the first sublinear upper bound for this problem. They also show that the established exponential mechanism can operate with O(√m) expected accesses. These results address the retrieval cost of private selection rather than treating access to all data as automatic.

Lower bounds distinguish algorithms restricted to random access, those restricted to sorted access, and those able to combine both. Avoiding an Ω(m) access cost requires support for both kinds of access. When both are available, the proposed algorithm's access cost is optimal. The result therefore links achievable efficiency directly to the data-access capabilities supplied by the underlying system.
icml-2023-tight-data-access-bounds-for-p.tldr: Private top-k selection achieves optimal O(√(mk)) expected data accesses when both random and sorted access are available.

paragraphs: Macro-AUC averages the AUC scores computed separately for each label in a multi-label problem. Although widely used, its generalization behavior has received limited theoretical treatment. This paper examines how the surrogate losses used to train different learning algorithms relate to performance on that evaluation measure beyond the training data.

The analysis identifies label-wise class imbalance as a critical factor in generalization bounds. For a given label, the balance between positive and negative examples affects the guarantees. The authors find that bounds for the widely used univariate-loss approach are more sensitive to this imbalance than those for their proposed pairwise and reweighted-loss approaches.

That difference suggests potentially worse performance for the univariate approach; the bound comparison alone does not make the performance ordering universal. Experiments across several datasets corroborate the theoretical findings. To establish the analysis, the authors also introduce a more general McDiarmid-type concentration inequality. The work connects a dataset property, the training loss, and the generalization behavior of a practical multi-label metric.
icml-2023-towards-understanding-generali.tldr: Imbalance-aware bounds suggest that pairwise and reweighted losses generalize more favorably for Macro-AUC than a common univariate loss.

paragraphs: Optimizing a useful objective can be expensive when its gradients are difficult to obtain. This paper studies how a related, more accessible function can help. The central idea is to use that cheaper proxy for much of the optimization while still consulting the true objective to guide progress toward the intended solution.

The algorithm combines approximate proximal-point iterations on the proxy with relatively few stochastic gradients from the objective. Its theoretical guarantee depends on the smoothness of the difference between the two functions. If that difference is δ-smooth, the convergence rate matches stochastic gradient descent on a δ-smooth objective.

This makes the relationship between the proxy and the objective central to the potential efficiency gain. Under the stated condition, the method can substantially improve sample efficiency. The authors identify synthetic data, physics simulators, and mixtures of public and private data as potential applications. Those examples illustrate ways an accessible proxy might arise; the abstract presents them as opportunities for the algorithm rather than reported application-specific experimental results.
icml-2023-two-losses-are-better-than-one.tldr: A cheaper proxy can reduce expensive gradient use, with convergence governed by the smoothness of its difference from the true objective.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can approximate molecular calculations quickly and accurately on familiar molecular-dynamics data, yet make large errors on unfamiliar samples. Uncertainty estimation aims to communicate when predictions deserve less confidence. The paper examines what such estimates should provide specifically for molecular force fields, where prediction accuracy alone is insufficient.

The authors define six desiderata, divided equally between physics-informed and application-focused requirements. They survey existing uncertainty methods against those criteria and conclude that none satisfies the full set. Their proposed Localized Neural Kernel, or LNK, extends existing GNNs using a Gaussian-process-based construction designed to satisfy all six.

The evaluation compares four uncertainty methods with three model backbones across two datasets. For out-of-equilibrium detection, LNK achieves up to 2.5 and 2.1 times lower errors measured in terms of AUC-ROC score than dropout and evidential-regression methods, respectively, while preserving high predictive performance. These results support combining domain-specific uncertainty requirements with a method that performs well on the reported detection task.
icml-2023-uncertainty-estimation-for-mol.tldr: LNK adds Gaussian-process-based uncertainty to molecular GNNs, satisfying six proposed criteria and improving reported out-of-equilibrium detection.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model during inference using an unlabeled batch, helping it respond to unfamiliar data distributions. This paper identifies a security consequence of that shared adaptation process: malicious inputs in a batch can affect predictions on other inputs that are benign and have not themselves been modified.

The proposed Distribution Invading Attack injects a small fraction of malicious data into the test batch. By exploiting the adaptation mechanism, it causes misclassification of unperturbed benign samples. The important distinction is where the attack acts: it changes the batch used for adaptation, creating an indirect route to influence predictions on separate samples.

Evaluations across multiple benchmarks and six adaptation methods demonstrate high attack effectiveness. The authors also investigate two countermeasures intended to strengthen existing implementations, following a security-by-design principle. The findings expose a utility-security tradeoff in the evaluated adaptation pipelines: using incoming data to improve predictions can also let malicious batch members influence them. They motivate considering this interaction when designing robust test-time adaptation.
icml-2023-uncovering-adversarial-risks-o.tldr: Malicious samples can exploit test-time adaptation to cause errors on untouched benign samples in the same batch.

paragraphs: Reducing language-model weights and activations to four-bit integers promises lower deployment costs, but higher peak hardware throughput does not automatically establish useful end-to-end speedups. This paper studies W4A4 quantization, asking both whether model accuracy survives the change and whether an optimized inference pipeline can realize the performance opportunity.

The accuracy findings differ by architecture. Encoder-only and encoder-decoder models show no or negligible degradation, whereas decoder-only models suffer a significant drop. The authors develop an optimized end-to-end W4A4 encoder inference pipeline supporting different quantization strategies, connecting the numerical representation to an implementation that delivers measured speed gains.

Compared with FP16 inference, the pipeline is 8.5 times faster in latency-oriented scenarios and up to three times faster in throughput-oriented scenarios. It also improves on FasterTransformer's state-of-the-art BERT INT8 performance by up to 1.7 times. The study further examines decoder-only failure cases and compatibility with pruning and layer reduction. Its findings make architecture and execution setting central to interpreting the benefits of INT4.
icml-2023-understanding-int4-quantizatio.tldr: W4A4 quantization delivers substantial encoder inference speedups, while the studied decoder-only models suffer significant accuracy loss.
